extracted.intended_audience: authors and readers of true-crime / criminological narratives (crime writers, historians, journalists)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for selecting, researching, and writing non‑fiction accounts of criminals (here focused on women): emphasizes source criticism, tone, selection of cases, and restrained psychological comment. Suited to writers of popular criminology and true‑crime essays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid facetiousness and puerile humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not treat serious criminal material with frivolous humour or pedantry (e.g., avoid joking or flippant titles that risk libel or trivialization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes an initial impulse to call the book 'Pale Hands' or 'Fair Hands Imbrued' and discards it to avoid 'pedant or puerile humour' and danger of libel. Choose titles and turns of phrase that respect the seriousness of the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine and verify sources; practice conscientious source criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Rigorously check the sources of information; many historical accusations are contaminated by political rancour, bias, or calumny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author insists 'it behoves the conscientious writer to examine the sources of his information' and points out partisan writers and translators often distort facts. Use original juridical records, eyewitness accounts, and contemporary documents where possible; do not rely unquestioningly on later secondary treatments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer eyewitness and primary records over second‑hand rechauffage
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible, rely on the eyewitness or contemporary record rather than later writers who 'rechauffe' material and may add darker meanings in translation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the contrast between Boccaccio (eyewitness) and Infessura (who was not present) is given to show how later writers attach 'the darkest meanings' to festivities and produce calumny. Seek out trial reports, letters, diaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of translation and re-telling bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Translators and later retellers often intensify or alter meanings; be cautious of assertions that arise from translation or partisan interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns that 'rechauffeurs ... apt ... to attach the darkest meanings to the words they translate' and gives examples (Borgias, Lucretia) where translation/retelling produced lurid reputations. Note provenance and language issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid libelous or unsubstantiated allegations; respect legal outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assert guilt where it is unproven; be careful about naming as guilty those who were acquitted or where charges are doubtful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author excludes some women because 'several were assoiled of the charges against them' and says his facetious title 'put me in peril of libel.' State legal outcomes clearly and avoid definitive accusations when evidence is lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use restrained, modest psychological comment ('a soupçon of psychology')
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit speculative psychological analysis to a small, tasteful amount; do not over‑psychologize historical actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author promises only 'a soupçon of psychology'—just enough to serve transitions from narrative to analysis. Keep psychological deductions concise and proportionate to the evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid romanticizing or sensationalizing crime; eschew superlatives and honorifics
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat crime as sordid, not glamorous: avoid labels like 'master criminal', 'queen' or excessive superlatives that gild or idealize wrongdoers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author objects to the use of honorifics ('queens' etc.) and says 'there is no romance in crime... Crime is never anything but a sordid business.' Maintain a sober, unsentimental tone and resist sensational flourish for popularity's sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for balanced tone: neither pity nor contempt
rubrics_metrics.description: Present criminals as human beings; do not ask readers simply to pity or to condemn—seek a balanced human interest perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author writes he will not ask the reader 'to view the criminal with the thought attributed to John Knox' and instead seeks something between pity and contempt. Avoid moral grandstanding; present context, motives, and facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select cases with genuine points of interest and available records
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose cases that offer substantive material for criminological study—cases with documentary records, interesting legal or social features, or instructive motives—rather than those already exhausted or purely sensational.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes 'there is no case of murder proved and accepted as such which does not contain its points of interest' and complains about overworked subjects. Novelty, accessibility of sources, and criminological value should guide selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be honest and transparent about limitations and biases in the record
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge when material is thin, partisan, or uncertain; make readers aware of possible political rancour, envy, or calumny influencing accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preface repeatedly points out that accusations can be founded on 'mere envy' or partisan motives and that later writers may embellish. State limitations, conflicting accounts, and provenance to allow readers to judge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not fictionalize or add unnecessary invented detail to historical/scriptural narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid creating fictional embellishment for well‑known historical or scriptural figures where the original accounts are already adequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author declines to add fictional detail to biblical stories ('Their stories are plainly and excellently told in the Scriptural manner, and the adding of detail would be mere fictional exercise'). Respect the form and sufficiency of primary narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rely on juridical records and trial reports as core source material
rubrics_metrics.description: Use assize reports, coroners' inquests, trial transcripts, post‑mortems and other legal records as essential evidentiary bases for true‑crime accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Throughout the preface the author refers to 'contemporary juridical records', 'trial reports', 'post‑mortem' findings (e.g., arsenic discovered, exhumations) as central evidence. Prioritize these primary legal documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider socioeconomic and physical contexts as explanatory factors rather than moral failings
rubrics_metrics.description: When accounting for criminal behaviour (especially among women), weigh economic pressures, physical differences, and social circumstances as explanatory elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that 'reasons for this are patent. They are economic reasons usually, and physical,' when explaining some female descent into crime. Use context to explain rather than simply condemn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid manufactured sensational detail to attract readership; prefer honest artistry
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not invent or exaggerate lurid episodes for popularity; rely on good writing and careful selection rather than superlative hyperbole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author criticizes writers who add 'piquant sauces' and says 'I loathe the use of superlatives in serious works on crime.' Aim for decency in treatment and craft rather than sensational merchandising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame and title works to prevent misinterpretation or legal risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose framing devices and titles that do not overstate accusations or invite libel claims; be mindful of how phrasing may mislead about guilt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The initial abandoned title and concern 'my proposed facetiousness put me in peril of libel' illustrate that framing/titling can create legal and ethical problems. Ensure language is accurate and cautious.
